title: TSMC Customer Capacity Expansion: 2026 Update
abstract: A named broker's channel checks point to a shift in how the foundry's largest customers are securing wafer supply for the coming cycle.
body:
## TSMC Customer Capacity Expansion: 2026 Update

On 2026-04-22, analysts at KGI Securities in Taipei circulated a revised note on TSMC's customer-driven capacity expansion, arguing that the foundry's largest accounts have moved from opportunistic booking to contractual lock-in for advanced nodes. The note, authored by semiconductor analyst Laura Chen, raises KGI's 2026 capital expenditure estimate for TSMC to $42.5 billion from $38.0 billion, citing customer prepayments and equipment lead times that now stretch to 52 weeks for extreme ultraviolet lithography tools.

The revision follows a March quarter in which TSMC reported revenue of NT$892.4 billion, up 34 percent year over year, with high performance computing accounting for 59 percent of sales. Chen wrote that the composition of demand has changed materially since the 2024 cycle, when inventory corrections at smartphone customers masked the scale of AI-related orders. "The current expansion is not a broad restocking event," Chen wrote. "It is a concentrated build-out tied to a handful of customers who are willing to fund capacity ahead of demand."

## The Anchor Tenants

Nvidia remains the single largest driver of leading-edge demand, according to the KGI note. The broker estimates Nvidia has committed to roughly 180,000 wafer starts per month at TSMC's N3 and N2 nodes by the fourth quarter of 2026, up from approximately 110,000 in the fourth quarter of 2025. That figure includes both the Blackwell Ultra family and the first volume production of the Rubin architecture, which KGI expects to tape out at N2 in the third quarter of 2026.

Apple, by contrast, is described as a steady but no longer dominant customer at the leading edge. KGI estimates Apple's share of TSMC's N3 capacity will fall to 28 percent by the end of 2026 from 41 percent a year earlier, as Nvidia and AMD absorb newly installed tool capacity. Apple's A20 processor, expected in the iPhone 18 family, will remain on N3P, a performance-enhanced variant, rather than moving to N2, according to supply chain checks. Chen noted that this decision reduces Apple's cost per wafer but cedes the earliest access to N2 to competitors.

AMD is the fastest-growing customer in percentage terms. KGI estimates AMD's wafer commitments at TSMC will rise 62 percent in 2026, driven by the MI400 accelerator series and server CPU demand. The broker places AMD's N2 bookings at 35,000 wafer starts per month by the fourth quarter, a figure that would make AMD the second-largest N2 customer after Nvidia.

## The Japanese Anchor

The most consequential new commitment, according to the note, comes from a Japanese consortium led by Sony and Toyota, which has signed a multiyear agreement for N2 capacity at TSMC's Kumamoto fab, known formally as JASM. KGI estimates the consortium's initial volume at 12,000 wafer starts per month beginning in the first quarter of 2027, with an option to double that figure by 2028. The chips are intended for automotive vision processors and industrial robotics controllers, applications that have historically lagged the leading edge by two or three nodes.

Chen argued that this agreement is significant less for its volume than for its structure. The consortium has agreed to prepay 40 percent of the wafer cost over the first 18 months, a departure from TSMC's traditional pay-as-you-ship model. "This is the first time a Japanese customer group has taken prepayment risk on leading-edge capacity," Chen wrote. "It signals that automotive customers now view advanced nodes as a strategic input rather than a commodity."

The Bank of Japan's monetary policy stance enters the analysis indirectly. KGI notes that yen weakness through 2025 improved the economics of JASM's exports but that a gradual normalization by the BoJ could compress margins for the consortium. Chen does not forecast a BoJ rate path but flags currency as a risk to the prepayment structure.

## Equipment and Packaging Constraints

The capacity expansion is constrained less by cleanroom space than by packaging. KGI estimates that TSMC's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity will reach 66,000 wafers per month by the fourth quarter of 2026, up from 38,000 a year earlier, but that demand for CoWoS from Nvidia alone will exceed 70,000 wafers per month in the same period. The shortfall, Chen wrote, will persist into 2027 and is the primary reason Nvidia has qualified alternative packaging suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea.

Equipment lead times reinforce the bottleneck. ASML's EUV tools now carry a 52-week lead time, and KGI reports that TSMC has placed orders for 28 EUV systems for delivery in 2026, up from 19 in 2025. High-NA EUV tools, which TSMC has been slower to adopt than Intel, remain a 2027 story, according to the note.

## What to Watch

KGI's revised model assumes no recession and no escalation of export controls affecting TSMC's China-based customers. Chen identifies three signposts for the second half of 2026: TSMC's monthly revenue reports for June and July, which will reveal whether N2 ramp is tracking ahead of schedule; Nvidia's data center gross margin, which will show whether the company is absorbing higher wafer and packaging costs; and the JASM consortium's first tool move-in, scheduled for August 2026.

A rival note from Morgan Stanley, published on 2026-04-18, takes a more cautious view, arguing that customer prepayments are a form of vendor financing that flatters near-term cash flow while obscuring demand risk. Morgan Stanley maintains a 2026 capex estimate of $39.5 billion for TSMC. The gap between the two houses, roughly $3 billion, is the clearest measure of how much of the current expansion is contracted versus anticipated.

TSMC declined to comment on customer-specific capacity figures. The company's next earnings call is scheduled for 2026-07-16.
